import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 985

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/985](https://www.erdosproblems.com/985)
-/

namespace Erdos985

/--
Is it true that, for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q \leq p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_985 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (p : ℕ) (hp_prime : p.Prime) (hp_nontrivial : p ≠ 2),
    ∃ q, q.Prime ∧ q < p ∧ orderOf (q : ZMod p) = p - 1 := by
  sorry

-- TODO: Artin conjectured that 2 is a primitive root for infinitely many primes $p$, which
-- Hooley proved assuming the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis.

/--
Heath-Brown proved that at least one of 2, 3, or 5 is a primitive root for infinitely many primes $p$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_985.variants.two_three_five_primitive_root :
    Set.Infinite
      {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧
      (orderOf (2 : ZMod p) = p - 1 ∨
       orderOf (3 : ZMod p) = p - 1 ∨
       orderOf (5 : ZMod p) = p - 1)} := by
  sorry

end Erdos985

findings.description: The docstring says “for every prime p”, but the theorem explicitly assumes `p ≠ 2`. This exception matters to the prose: at p = 2, the only prime q ≤ p is 2, whose residue is zero and has order 0, not p − 1 = 1. The Lean restriction appropriately removes this automatic counterexample; the docstring should make it explicit. The separate difference between q ≤ p in the docstring and q < p in Lean is harmless, since q = p cannot be a primitive root.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/985 likewise says “for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q<p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$”, without spelling out the necessary exception. The main page records the problem as OPEN. Thus the source shares this boundary omission; this is a documentation clarification, not a recommendation to restore p = 2 to the Lean statement.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to ask about “every odd prime p” (or “every prime p > 2”) and use q < p. Leave the theorem’s `p ≠ 2` hypothesis intact.

reformulations.difference: The primitive-root condition is expressed using `orderOf (q : ZMod p) = p - 1` in the multiplicative monoid of the ring, rather than explicitly requiring a generator of its unit group.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For prime p, p − 1 is positive. Having this order forces the residue of q to be a unit. Its order in the ring equals its order in the unit group, whose cardinality is p − 1; consequently it generates that group exactly when the displayed equality holds. The equivalence with the existence of such a unit generator was proved as `Review985.order_iff_generator`.

reformulations.difference: Lean asserts that infinitely many primes have at least one of 2, 3, and 5 as a primitive root. The source says that one fixed member of this triple is a primitive root for infinitely many primes.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The Lean set is the union of the three sets of primes corresponding to 2, 3, and 5. A finite union is infinite exactly when at least one constituent is infinite. Combined with the order characterization of primitive roots, this gives precisely the source’s fixed-choice assertion. The full equivalence with `∃ a ∈ ({2, 3, 5} : Finset ℕ), ...` was proved as `Review985.heath_brown_fixed_choice`.

review.notes: No substantive mathematical statement defect was found. The source’s open status and its attribution of the solved variant to Heath-Brown agree with both category tags. The unspecified propositional answer has the correct scope. Prime hypotheses exclude the exceptional moduli 0 and 1 and make natural subtraction and the order-zero convention harmless. `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` compiles successfully; it proves the reported equivalences, equivalence of the strict/non-strict witness bounds, and failure of the unrestricted docstring at p = 2. A computable bounded-order test, proved equivalent to the order condition for p > 1, was evaluated for every prime through 31. The reviewed file was not modified.
